tagline.text: Where General Yamashita surrendered, a WWII shrine shaped like an Ifugao house

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (part of a Kiangan day trip)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (per day locally, excluding round-trip transport from Manila)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: A national landmark on a hill in Kiangan town, the shrine was built in 1974 on the site where Japanese General Tomoyuki Yamashita surrendered in 1945. From the roof of the concrete building, modeled on an Ifugao house, you can see all around Kiangan.

The Ifugao War Memorial Shrine (Bantayog sa Kiangan, also called the Kiangan National Shrine or Yamashita Shrine) is a memorial park in Barangay Linda, Kiangan, Ifugao. It is known as the place where General Tomoyuki Yamashita, commander of the Imperial Japanese Army in the Philippines, surrendered to the Allied forces, effectively ending the Japanese occupation of the country. The Philippine Tourism Authority built it in

and it was dedicated in 1975. On July 9 of that year President Marcos declared it a military shrine by Proclamation No. 1460, and it is now run by the Philippine Veterans Affairs Office (PVAO). The National Historical Commission has declared the site a National Landmark.

A little history makes the visit more meaningful. Late in the war in 1945, Yamashita's forces were pushed into the mountains of northern Luzon and held out around Kiangan, and the combined operations of American and Filipino troops and recognized guerrillas, together with cut supply lines, are said to have steadily reduced them. He then surrendered at Kiangan, and English Wikipedia places this on 2 September 1945, the day of Japan's formal surrender. The shrine keeps that story alive. The grounds are also said to be where an American lieutenant governor set up the headquarters of U.S. military and civil authority in 1910.

The most striking feature is the shrine building, a giant version of a traditional Ifugao house. Made of steel and concrete with a pyramid-like roof, it is the tallest structure in the compound. A wooden relief carved with scenes from the war covers a wall inside, and an entrance at the back leads up to a rooftop viewpoint. From the roof, green mountains stretch out over Kiangan town, the surrounding barangays, and in the distance toward Lagawe.

In the middle of the compound are a parade ground with a covered grandstand and a lawn, and the museum stands at the far end. Victory Day ceremonies are held here every September 2, a good time to visit together with Kiangan's local festival, Gotad ad Kiyangan. Sources differ on whether the surrender happened on September 2 or 3, so this guide follows the local observance of September 2. Many itineraries show only the rice terraces of Banaue or Batad, but Kiangan lets you see Ifugao culture and modern history together. The shrine is small, so 1–2 hours is enough, and combined with the nearby Nagacadan Rice Terraces or a walk through an Ifugao village it makes a half-day or full-day trip.

blocks.title: A shrine shaped like an Ifugao house

children.text: The building is an enlarged version of a traditional Ifugao house with a conical roof, built in steel and concrete. As the tallest building in the compound, it is visible from far away. For photos, stand at the foot of the front steps so the whole building fits in the frame. The space under the roof echoes the structure of a real Ifugao house, so it is fun to compare it with houses in the village.

An entrance at the back of the building leads to the rooftop viewpoint. To one side are mountains, and to the other the Ifugao lowlands and Kiangan town. The light is soft late in the afternoon, which makes for good photos. It can be windy near the railing, so keep a firm hold on your hat and small belongings.

Climb the steps inside the shrine and you will find a wooden carving covering one wall. It depicts scenes from the war and is where the Ifugao woodcarving tradition meets memorial architecture. Whether the interior is open can vary by day, so follow the on-site instructions.

In the middle of the compound are a covered grandstand and a wide lawn. Performances and ceremonies are held here on Victory Day and during local events. On ordinary days it is quiet and pleasant for a rest.

The museum stands at the far end of the compound and covers Ifugao culture and history. Photography is said to be restricted inside, so check at the entrance. Opening hours are best confirmed locally.

blocks.title: Victory Day and Gotad ad Kiyangan

children.text: Victory Day ceremonies are held in the compound every September 2. The Gotad ad Kiyangan festival, Kiangan's signature event, is also listed around this time. Exact dates and programs change every year, so ask the Kiangan tourism office.

blocks.title: A walk through town and the school road

children.text: From the Kiangan municipal hall, climb the hill along the road toward Kiangan Central School and Ifugao Academy and you reach the shrine entrance. The walk takes about
10–15 minutes
, and you pass the market, schools and a church on the way up.
Arrive in Kiangan town and have breakfast. The shrine is said to open daily at
, so going early keeps it quiet.
Walk up from the municipal hall or take a tricycle to the shrine entrance. First walk once around the compound to see the parade ground and the outside of the building.
See the relief inside the shrine, then climb the back stairs to the rooftop viewpoint. Take your time with the view over Kiangan.
Visit the museum at the far end of the compound to see Ifugao culture and local history.
Go back down to town for lunch and, if needed, catch a jeepney toward Lagawe or Banaue.
The shrine alone takes 1–2 hours, so adding nearby rice terraces the same day is an efficient plan.

items.title: Full-day plan
items.subtitle: The shrine and Nagacadan Rice Terraces

children.text: See the shrine first and use the rooftop viewpoint to get a feel for Kiangan's terrain.
Find a guide or a tricycle in town and head to the Nagacadan Rice Terraces. Always agree on the fare before you leave.
Have lunch in town or at a village eatery.
Return to town and prepare to head toward Lagawe or Banaue. Jeepneys become scarce after dark, so do not leave it too late.
Check entrance and guide fees for the Nagacadan Rice Terraces and Kiangan's other attractions with the Kiangan tourism office.

Take an overnight Ifugao-bound bus from the Ohayami Trans terminal in Sampaloc, Manila. The service once ran straight to Kiangan, but some guides say it now goes only as far as Lagawe, so confirm the destination when you book.
The trip takes about
9–10 hours

From Lagawe to Kiangan it is about
10 km
, roughly
15 minutes
by road.
Schedules and fares change often. Check directly with the bus company before you leave.

items.title: By private car or rental from Manila

children.text: One route follows the Eastern Highway toward San Jose, and the trip is described as about
350 km
and
9 hours
The road is a two-lane mountain road with many sharp curves. Do not confuse it with the western route via Baguio and Sagada; Kiangan lies on the east side of the Central Cordillera.
From Lagawe, take a tricycle or jeepney to Kiangan. An older source puts a shared tricycle at about
per person, so confirm the current fare locally.
From Banaue to Lagawe by jeepney is said to take about
30 minutes–1.5 hours
, and jeepneys leave from near the market.
From the Kiangan municipal hall, climb the hill toward the central school, then take the second road on the right to reach the shrine entrance. It is about a
10–15 minute
walk.
If you have luggage or the day is hot, take a tricycle.
The dry season from November to May is the best time to explore Ifugao. The rooftop view is the highlight here, so go on a day with little fog or rain.
Around Victory Day on September 2 there are events and more to see, but it falls in the rainy season, so the weather is changeable and the compound can be crowded.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Good for rooftop views and photos. Mornings and evenings can be chilly.
Midday sun is strong, so visit early in the morning.
Victory Day ceremonies on September 2; take care on mountain roads.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Kiangan town has small guesthouses and homestays. For more choice, many travelers stay in Lagawe or Banaue and visit as a day trip. Book ahead in peak season.
Town eateries serve local rice, chicken dishes and vegetables from the hills. Ifugao rice has a famous name, so be sure to have at least one meal with rice.

The shrine visit is short, so choose your lodging to fit your rice terrace trekking plans. Banaue has many guesthouses with views, while Kiangan and Lagawe are quieter. Restaurant hours and lodging rates change by season, so confirm locally.
Go up to the rooftop viewpoint in the morning, when the light is good, for a clear view toward town.
The shrine is both an Ifugao cultural site and a war memorial, so visit quietly.
Photography inside the museum may be restricted, so ask at the entrance first.
Carry small change (₱20, 50, 100) for tricycles and donations.
Combining the visit with the Nagacadan Rice Terraces makes for a full day. Agree on the transport fare before you leave.
The dates and program of Victory Day (September 2) and local festivals vary each year, so ask the Kiangan tourism office before you go.
Overnight buses from Manila get cold, so bring a light jacket.
After the shrine, a slow walk along the school and market streets shows everyday Ifugao life. Ask people first before taking their photo.
Fees and hours differ between sources, so the safest approach is to phone or email the municipal tourism office for the latest information.
Entrance fees, opening hours, museum access and whether the Manila bus goes straight to Kiangan differ between sources, so confirm locally before you go.
Mountain roads can see landslides and closures in the rainy season, so check the latest road conditions before leaving.
The shrine is a place of remembrance. Avoid loud noise and inappropriate behavior.
The rooftop stairs can be narrow and steep, so watch for slippery steps after rain.
ATMs are scarce in this area, so bring cash in advance.
Jeepneys and tricycles become scarce after dark, so head back before it gets late.
There is little shade in the compound at midday. Bring a hat and water.
